title: Honitsu routing / calling / value drill items

notation.tile: number + suit letter. m = manzu, p = pinzu, s = souzu. Trailing 'r' = red five, e.g. '5mr'.
notation.honors: E S W N = East South West North. P = haku (white). F = hatsu (green). C = chun (red).
notation.meld: { tiles: [...] in display order with the CALLED tile first, called: <index>, kind: 'chi'|'pon' }

answer_model: Every item has options[] with exactly one correct:true, plus a rationale string. Render prompt + hand, take the answer, then show rationale. Type-specific fields are extra context, not required to score.

types.routing: Pick the road: riichi (play straight/closed) | hedge | honitsu.
types.calling: A tile is offered. Call it (and with which tiles) or pass.
types.value_gate: Count the han this hand yields as-is, and identify the second source.

items.prompt: Which road is this hand on?
items.rationale: Stop 1. The hatsu triplet is a finished set AND a yaku at the same time. Riichi + hatsu + ura reaches mangan with nothing forced, so there is no case for chasing honitsu — you would be pulling apart a hand already on the strongest road.

items.prompt: Manzu looks heavy. Which road?
items.rationale: Stop 2. 4p5p and 7s8s are two ryanmen in two different suits — the hand already has speed. Honitsu means cutting both and rebuilding a wait from nothing. Ponning the chun for 1,000 is also acceptable; a cheap fast hand still ends a dealership. Compare item r-05: same shape family, but there the honors make it mangan and the ruling flips.

items.prompt: Eight manzu tiles. Which road?
items.rationale: Stop 3. 3s4s5s is already a finished set. Demolishing a completed block is the most expensive thing you can do to a hand, and honitsu is not worth that price when riichi is available. Note the manzu count is genuinely tempting here — eight tiles — which is exactly why this one catches people.

items.prompt: Which road?
items.rationale: Trigger A. Played straight this reaches tenpai roughly never. Honitsu converts a dead hand into a live one, and the five honors you are holding double as fold stock — unusual for an open hand. Value check also clears: the chun pair means honitsu + chun = 3 han minimum.

items.prompt: Two off-suit ryanmen here. Which road?

options.label: Riichi — Stop 2 says keep the ryanmen

items.rationale: Trigger B overrides Stop 2. Yes, 4p5p and 7s8s are two ryanmen — but look at the honors: haku pair AND chun pair. Honitsu 2 + haku 1 + chun 1 = 4 han = mangan. Stop 2 was never 'don't break ryanmen', it was 'don't break ryanmen for a CHEAP honitsu'. Caveat: both pairs must become triplets for the full 4 han. One landing gives 3 han (~3,900-5,200), which still clears the gate.

items.prompt: Which road?
items.rationale: Trigger B via red five. Honitsu 2 + chun 1 + red five 1 = 4 han. The red five does the work a good shape would otherwise have to, so cutting both off-suit ryanmen still lands mangan. Note this is the MORE reliable version of trigger B than r-05: the red five is already in your hand, whereas a dragon pair still has to complete.

items.prompt: Chun is ponned. Which road from here?

options.label: Cut the haku — take the fastest tenpai
Keep the haku — hedge on it pairing

items.rationale: Hedge. This is ryanmen-ryanmen iishanten (1m1m pair, 789m set, 6m7m, 2s3s, chun set) with the lone haku as a sixth block held purely for value. Pair the haku and you are honitsu + chun + haku, a completely different hand. Rule: tenpai first, take it; haku first, shift. This is Gentaro Q8-4 with a dragon instead of a pin block.

items.prompt: Same hand as r-07. You draw a 3s. What do you discard?
items.rationale: This is what 'paying for the option' actually looks like, and it is sharper than it sounds. 233s is a genuinely useful shape — backup pair, upgrade path. The efficient discard is the haku. You throw the 3s anyway. The lesson is not 'discard junk to keep your option', it is 'decline a real improvement to keep the value route open' (打点をおう). If optionality only ever costs you worthless tiles, you are not hedging, you are holding a floater until it becomes inconvenient.

items.prompt: Six manzu tiles and an honor pair. Which road?
items.rationale: The value gate as a hard veto. Seat and round wind are both East, so North, South and West are all GUEST winds — zero han. Honitsu here is 2 han, ~2,000. Meanwhile 234m and 567m are already complete, plus two ryanmen and a pair. You would be paying two finished runs' worth of structure for 2,000 points. Contrast r-10: same absence of yakuhai, opposite answer, because there the hand has nothing to pay with.

items.prompt: No dragons, no dora, all guest winds. Which road?
items.rationale: The hardest item here, and the one that shows the gate is ASYMMETRIC. Honitsu is only 2 han — but the alternative is noten. You are paying nothing because there is nothing to pay with, so the gate stops being a veto and becomes a throttle: it tells you HOW HARD to push, not whether to start. Correct play is take the free calls, hold the honor pairs for defense, and fold the moment anyone riichis. Compare r-09, where the identical value picture produces the opposite ruling because good blocks were on the table.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. A 7m is discarded. Call it?
items.note: Partial hand — only the relevant block is shown.
items.rationale: Kuinobashi. Chi with 5m6m and you keep a live 4m5m ryanmen while locking 567m. Four tiles became a set plus a working ryanmen. Compare c-04, which is the same four tiles called wrong.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. A 3m is discarded. Call it?
items.note: Partial hand — only the relevant block is shown.
items.rationale: Kuinobashi. Chi with 2m4m locks 234m and leaves 2m3m as a live ryanmen.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. A 7m is discarded. Call it?
items.note: Partial hand — only the relevant block is shown.
items.rationale: Kuinobashi. Chi with 8m9m locks 789m and leaves 6m7m as a live ryanmen. Calling with 6m8m instead would leave 7m9m — a kanchan. Same tiles, worse outcome.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. A 5m is discarded. Call it?
items.note: Partial hand — only the relevant block is shown.
items.rationale: Never 1 — the shape-wrecking call. Ponning the 5m leaves you on a 4-6m kanchan. Identical four tiles to c-01, and the only difference is which tiles you called with. Take it only if it is clear you will not reach tenpai otherwise, and reluctantly.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. A 5m is discarded. Call it?
items.note: Partial hand — only the relevant block is shown.
items.rationale: Never 1 — the shape-wrecking call. Chi with 6m7m and you are left on an 8-9m penchan. Same four tiles as c-03, called wrong.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu, chun ponned. A 6m is discarded — but you already hold 5m6m7m as a finished run. Call it?
items.rationale: Call it. The shanten does NOT improve — 567m was already a finished run. What the call buys is one manzu tile from outside your hand: working manzu goes from 112m to 1126m, and the spare 6m becomes a fifth-block seed (456m, 678m, 66m) where the locked run had nowhere to go. Volume in the suit is worth paying for even when it does not shorten the hand, because a suit tile you called is a suit tile you never have to draw. Discard the 9s. Value clears easily: honitsu 2 + chun 1 + haku 1 = mangan.

items.prompt: Honitsu-only, no yakuhai. A West is discarded and you hold two. Pon it?

options.label: Pass — keep the pair as safe tiles

items.rationale: Never 2 — bakahon. Seat and round wind are East, so West and North are guest winds: this hand is honitsu-only, 2 han, ~2,000 points. Ponning the West raises the ceiling and drops your defense to zero. Leave the pair as fold stock — that defensive reserve is the entire reason scattered-hand honitsu was attractive. Do not sell safe tiles this cheaply.

items.prompt: Same hand as c-07 — but you are now the West seat. A West is discarded. Pon it?

options.label: Pass — keep the pair as safe tiles

items.rationale: The exception, and the reason the rule is worded carefully. West is now YOUR seat wind, so the pon adds a han: honitsu 2 + seat wind 1 = 3 han, mangan-adjacent with any dora. At that value, burning your defense to push is correct. The rule was never 'protect your safe tiles' — it is 'do not sell your safe tiles CHEAPLY'. Identical tiles to c-07, opposite answer, and the only thing that changed is your seat.

items.prompt: Open manzu honitsu, completed as shown. How many han?

answer.verdict: no second source — do not pay blocks for this

items.rationale: Honitsu 2 and nothing else. North is a guest wind at East seat / East round, so the triplet is worth zero han. This is the shape of the trap: eight turns of work for ~2,000 points.

items.prompt: Open manzu honitsu, completed as shown. How many han?

answer.verdict: clears the gate — a real hand

items.rationale: Honitsu 2 + chun 1 = 3 han. One dragon triplet roughly doubles the payout over v-01. This is the minimum you should accept when you are paying real blocks for the road.

items.prompt: Open manzu honitsu, completed as shown. How many han?

answer.verdict: mangan — stop optimising the wait and push

items.rationale: Honitsu 2 + haku 1 + chun 1 = 4 han = mangan. Note the wait is a lone East tanki, which is terrible and does not matter. Once a hand is mangan-class, stop optimising the wait and push whatever you are given — a bad wait on 8,000 beats a good wait on 2,000.

items.prompt: Open manzu honitsu, completed as shown. You are the South seat in the East round. How many han?
items.rationale: Honitsu 2 + South as your seat wind 1 = 3 han. The same triplet would be worth zero to any other player at the table — this is why 'is it a guest wind?' has to be part of the value check, not just 'is it an honor?'. If you were South seat in the South round it would be a double wind: 4 han and mangan.

items.prompt: Committed to manzu honitsu. If you won RIGHT NOW on this shape, how many han?

options.label: 2 han — the pairs are not yet triplets

answer.verdict: 4 han is the CEILING, not the current value

items.rationale: The most common miscount. Two dragon pairs is a CEILING of 4 han, not a floor — haku-haku is worth zero until it is haku-haku-haku. Right now this is 2 han. Land one dragon and you are at 3; land both and you are at 4. The commit is still correct because the ceiling is high, but plan for the 3-han outcome and treat mangan as upside. A dora or red five is a more reliable second source precisely because it is already in hand.

items.prompt: Open manzu honitsu, completed as shown. Dora is 8m. How many han?

answer.verdict: haneman — this is what stacking looks like

items.rationale: Honitsu 2 + chun 1 + two dora (the 8m pair) + red five 1 = 6 han, haneman. Worth drilling because it shows the upside the video never quantifies: honitsu's base of 2 is a MULTIPLIER PLATFORM, not a ceiling. Every han you stack on top roughly doubles again, which is why 'where is my second han?' is the right question and 'is honitsu possible?' is the wrong one.
